title: Reset a Perfection game: wind the timer round, press the pop-up tray down level
instruction: Get the Perfection game ready for the next player: tray down and held by its catches, timer set to 60 seconds and running, hands off.
context: Perfection (Hasbro Gaming, a 1973 classic) is the family game whose tray pops up when its 60 s timer runs out. Each turn starts from the same reset, in the game's own steps: switch to STOP, turn the dial clockwise to its stop, press the tray down, slide the switch to START. Three demands. Winding: the dial turns 300 degrees by its grip bar to its stop, more than a wrist turn: regrips. The level press: four springs push the 230 mm tray up with about 11.7 N where it holds, more than one arm's straight-down push (about 8 N); pushed on one side it rocks on its guides and only that side goes home, so two hands drive it down together near opposite edges, level, 25 mm. The order: left at START with the dial run out, the timer's cam keeps the tray from staying down (at STOP it may be pressed before or after winding). Then start it, let go. Unlike a jack-in-the-box reset (one lid, one catch), this is a timed sequence with a two-arm level press.
setup: Bimanual YAM station; units mm, heights above the table top; x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y to the robot's left, z up; arm bases at (0, +305) and (0, -305), arms in their ready pose with grippers open. (1) Game: Hasbro Gaming Perfection (25 shapes, 60 s timer), the game unit, and its 25 shapes standing ready, handles up, in the box lid behind the unit (lid 280 x 280, centred at (660, 0); not touched). The unit (a blue case 285 x 285 x 70 high) stands on the bare table centred at (330, 0), square to the robot, on tape marks, its front border (the dial and the switch) toward the robot. (2) Tray: yellow, 230 x 230, its 25 shape wells drawn on it, centred 20 behind the case's centre, so its edges run at y +115 and -115 and x 235 to 465. At the start it stands popped up, its top at 95 (25 proud of the case's deck at 70). Four coil springs under it push it up: about 3.8 N popped, 11.7 N at the catch line, rising 320 N/m; the tray weighs 150 g. It slides straight down on its guides and can rock up to 4 degrees about the front-to-back axis when one side is pushed harder. Its bottom stop is 5 below flush. (3) Catches: inside each side wall a sprung pawl hangs on a hinge along x; its tooth reaches 4 in over a barb on the tray's side skirt. Pressed down, a 45 degree bevel under each barb rides the pawl out (about 0.7 N more per side); 24.5 down, the barb passes under the tooth and the pawl snaps back over it, so the springs hold the tray 1 above flush. Each side catches only when that side is driven past its tooth. (4) Timer: a red dial 40 across at (211, -90) with a white grip bar across it, 10 high; 0 points at the robot. Turned clockwise (seen from above) it stops at 60 s (300 degrees); it turns against about 0.015 N m of friction. With the switch at START it runs back 5 degrees per second, 1 s per second; at STOP it stays where it is left. When it runs out to 0 with the switch at START, a cam holds both pawls open, so the tray pops and cannot be latched. (5) Switch: a white knob 8 x 8 x 9 at (211, -40) that slides 12 to the left from START to STOP and clicks into either end. At the start the dial reads 0 and the switch is at START (the last game ran out). Spring rates, the pawls, the rock and the friction are estimates (Fidelity). The layout is the same in every trial.
scoring: Judged from the trial video, a photo of the dial and switch at the end, and a steel rule. Caught (a side): that side's pawl tooth over its barb, so the tray side cannot rise; in a real trial the tray side stays within 2 of flush when the hands are off (rule against the deck at the left and right edges). Latched: both sides caught. Forced: a barb driven through a tooth (in a real trial a broken or bent catch) at any step. Set: the dial shows 50 s or more. Running: over the last 1 s the switch was at START and the dial turned back at least 2 degrees (the photo and the video). Released: on every step of the last 1 s every part of both grippers is 50 or more from the game. Score 0 for the rest of the trial if Forced. Otherwise the highest of: 1.0 if latched, set, running and released, held 1 s more; 0.7 if latched and set at the end (for example the clock not started, or a hand still on the game); 0.5 if latched at the end; 0.25 if one side was caught at some moment; 0.1 if the tray was ever pressed 10 or more down at its centre; otherwise 0. The untouched start (tray up, dial at 0, switch at START) scores exactly 0, and a tray held down by a gripper without its catches scores 0.1. The trial ends at the run limit or as soon as 1.0 is reached (the clock still has about 55 s to run, so the tray does not pop during the trial). Possible scores: 0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0.
fidelity: PhysX, 20 Hz control. The unit is fixed (presses go straight down; the dial takes under 0.02 N m). The tray is one rigid plate on a slide plus a 4 degree rock hinge; its springs are the slide's preloaded drive. Catches hold by contact. Declared rules: the spring preload, the clockwork (5 deg/s at START), the switch's detents, the run-out cam. Wells drawn; lid and shapes are scenery. Spring rates, forces, rock, catch sizes: estimates, to measure with a spring scale and calipers.
reset_notes: Slide the switch to START and let the dial run to 0: the tray pops by itself (or press the tray and let it pop). Check that the dial reads 0, the switch is at START, the tray stands 25 proud and the unit sits on its tape marks. Grippers open in the ready pose. Nothing is consumed; the shapes stay in the box lid, handles up.
